headline: Oil Slide Offsets Jobs Jolt; Rates Hold at Lows
tileReason: The daily 30-year average held at 7.17% Friday, its lowest since late September, despite a much stronger jobs report; oil is falling again this morning ahead of Tuesday's inflation report.
takeaway:
Mortgage rates are holding at their lowest since late September. The daily 30-year average was unchanged Friday at 7.17%, the same as Thursday and the lowest since Sept 22. Freddie Mac's weekly survey is at 7.18% from last Thursday, its third straight weekly drop.

Friday's strong jobs report didn't knock rates off their lows. Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, roughly three times what forecasters expected, and unemployment dipped to 4.1%. Even so, the 10-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates tend to follow, rose only about 0.02% to close near 4.86%, still down about 0.08% for the week.

Lenders had room to absorb that small rise. The Optimal Blue conforming index, which tracks rates on loans borrowers actually locked, sat 2.25% above the 10-year Treasury on Nov 5, versus a long-run average of about 1.76%. That extra-wide gap gave lenders a cushion, so the average lender held pricing steady Friday.

Overnight and this morning, oil is falling again. U.S. crude is down about 3% to near $88 a barrel, and Brent slipped from about $98 at Friday's close to roughly $95 to $97, after an unconfirmed report that Iran softened its demands over the Strait of Hormuz and President Trump said more strikes are unlikely if talks progress. Weekend attacks on ships near the Strait keep that risk alive, but for now the 10-year yield is roughly flat near 4.85% to 4.87%, which points to steady lender pricing today.

A December Fed hike is still the base case. Futures markets, where traders bet on Fed decisions, put the odds of a quarter-point hike on Dec 9 at roughly 78% to 81% over the weekend, up from about 68% before Friday's jobs report; one outlet put it lower, just above 65%. Several Fed officials said last week that more hikes may be needed.

Tomorrow's inflation report is the next big test. Forecasters expect consumer prices rose about 0.3% in October, down from September's 0.6% jump, with core prices (which leave out food and energy) up about 0.2%. Because last year's government shutdown left a gap in the data, the report won't include the usual yearly inflation rate. The government also sells $125 billion of 3-, 10- and 30-year debt today, Tuesday and Thursday, and the bond market is closed Wednesday for Veterans Day.

fedOdds.title: Odds of a Fed hike on Dec 9
fedOdds.beforeLabel: Fri, Nov 6, before the jobs report

fedOdds.source: CME FedWatch via The Motley Fool (Nov 8); The Weekend Spread (Nov 6 close); TipRanks (Nov 9 morning)
fedOdds.note: CME FedWatch showed about 81% over the weekend, and Friday's close put it near 78%, up from about 68% before the jobs report. Sources differ: TipRanks this morning said market odds are just above 65% without naming its source. Either way, a hike is still seen as the most likely outcome.

drivers.title: Oil slides again on Iran talk hopes
drivers.text: U.S. crude fell about 3% this morning to near $88 a barrel after an unconfirmed report that Iran softened its demands over the Strait of Hormuz, and President Trump said more strikes on Iran are unlikely if talks progress. That follows a drop of about 16% in Brent last week. Cheaper oil lowers fuel and shipping costs and eases inflation worries, which helps bond yields and mortgage rates. Weekend attacks on ships near the Strait and doubts from Secretary of State Rubio mean this support can fade quickly.

drivers.title: October jobs report blows past forecasts
drivers.text: Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, about three times what forecasters expected, unemployment dipped to 4.1% and hourly pay rose 0.4%. A hot job market can keep wages, spending and inflation elevated, so investors sold some bonds Friday and the 10-year yield rose about 0.02% to near 4.86%. The rise was small enough that the daily mortgage average held at 7.17%.

drivers.title: December Fed hike odds near 78%-81%
drivers.text: Futures put the odds of a quarter-point Fed hike on Dec 9 at roughly 78% to 81% after the jobs report, up from about 68% before it, and several Fed officials said last week that more hikes may be needed. When investors expect higher short-term rates, longer-term rates, including mortgages, have a harder time falling. Tuesday's inflation report is the next big input.

drivers.title: Stock slump keeps money flowing to bonds
drivers.text: The S&P 500 had its worst week since April 2025, led by big losses in chip and tech stocks. When investors pull money out of stocks, some of it moves into bonds, which pushes yields down and helps mortgage rates. Stock futures are firmer this morning, so a rebound could reverse this support.

drivers.title: Mortgage rates still far above Treasuries
drivers.text: The Optimal Blue conforming index sat 2.25% above the 10-year Treasury yield on Nov 5, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That wide gap is a cushion: it let lenders hold rates steady after Friday's jobs report, and if markets calm down, there is room for mortgage rates to improve even if Treasury yields stay put.

outlook.basis: Still close to a coin flip, with a slight lean toward rates staying about where they are. Rates are at their lowest since late September and shrugged off a very strong jobs report, which suggests buyers of mortgage bonds are comfortable at these levels. In borrowers' favor: oil fell about 16% last week and is sliding again on Iran talk hopes, stocks are slumping, and mortgage rates are unusually far above the 10-year Treasury (about 2.25% vs. a long-run average near 1.76%). Working against them: a December Fed hike is seen as likely (about 78% to 81%), the job market is strong, inflation is well above target, and the Strait of Hormuz remains a flashpoint. Big swing events: Tuesday's October inflation report, this week's government bond sales, Iran headlines, the Nov 25 inflation report the Fed watches most closely, the Dec 4 jobs report and the Dec 9 Fed decision.
outlook.caveat: This is professional judgment from 30+ years watching these markets, not a guarantee. One oil headline or data surprise can move rates a quarter point in a day.

talkingPoints.buyers: The daily 30-year average is holding near 7.17%, its lowest since late September and down from roughly 7.5% in early October, even after a much stronger-than-expected jobs report Friday. Tuesday's inflation report could move rates either way, so it's worth talking with Stuart about how locking, a float-down option (which lets you take a lower rate if rates drop after you lock), or waiting would each fit your closing date.
talkingPoints.sellers: Rates have eased for three weeks, which helps affordability at the margin, but buyers are still stretched above 7%, and a strong economy and a likely December Fed hike could keep rates from falling much further. Realistic pricing, or a seller credit buyers can use to lower their rate, can help a home stand out.
talkingPoints.oneLiner: Mortgage rates are holding at their lowest since September, around 7.17%, even after a blowout jobs report; Tuesday's inflation report is the next big test.
